chunks: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who imposed oaths upon himself to walk to the Kaaba, or to give charity, or to free a slave, or a vow, or a sacrificial offering, if he were to speak to his father, or his mother, or his brother, or a relative, or [if he were to] cut off kinship ties, or a sin in which he persists, or a matter which is not proper for him to do.
So he (AS) said: 'The Book of God takes precedence over the oath, and there is no oath regarding disobedience.'

key_terms.أَيْمَان: Oaths (plural of yameen), legally binding sworn commitments in Islamic law
key_terms.كِتَابُ اللَّهِ: The Book of God (the Quran), which abrogates any oath that contradicts its commands
key_terms.مَعْصِيَة: Disobedience to God; an act categorized as sinful or forbidden in Islamic law

ai.seo_question: In Islam, is an oath to commit a sin or cut family ties binding?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses a man who bound himself with various religious obligations (walking to Mecca, giving charity, freeing a slave, fulfilling a vow, or presenting an offering) contingent on speaking with family members or committing sins. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) rules that the Quran, which commands maintaining family ties and forbids using oaths as pretexts for abandoning them, takes precedence over such oaths. The ruling encapsulates a foundational principle: an oath sworn to commit disobedience is legally void.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from usman Bin Isa, from Sama’at Bin Mahran who said, 
‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about a man who made up to himself an oath that he would walk to the Kaaba, or give charity, or freeing a slave, or a vow, or a gift, or an offering if he were to speak to his father, or his mother, or his brother, or a relative, or cutting off a relationship from his relative, or a transgression in which he is steadfast upon, or a matter which is not correct for him, so he does it’.
So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The Book of Allah<sup>azwj</sup> is before the oath, and there is no swearing of an oath with regards to a disobedience’.
en.sarwar: 7. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from ‘Uthman ibn ‘Isa from Sama‘ah ibn Mehran who has narrated the following: “I once asked abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a man who has taken an oath. He takes an oath to walk to al-Ka’bah or to pay charity or free a slave, vow, or to offer an offering animal if he speaks to his father or mother or his brother or a relative. Alternatively, he takes an oath to cut off relation with relatives or for an unlawful reason or something, which is not proper for him to do.
He (the Imam) said, ‘The Book of Allah is before taking an oath and there is no swearing in unlawful matters.’”
